content: If tuberculosis is resistant to isoniazid or rifampin but remains susceptible to ethionamide, ethionamide should be administered alongside at least one other drug to which the Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolate is known to be susceptible. If tuberculosis is resistant to both isoniazid and rifampin but still susceptible to ethionamide, the ethionamide must be combined with at least two other drugs to which the M. tuberculosis isolate is susceptible. Directly observed therapy (DOT) is recommended for all patients undergoing tuberculosis treatment. Baseline and periodic monitoring of liver function tests (LFTs), thyroid function tests (TFTs), and blood glucose levels are necessary during treatment. Ethionamide and cycloserine, when used together, may increase each other’s toxicity due to pharmacodynamic synergy, potentially leading to enhanced central nervous system (CNS) toxicity and an increased risk of seizures. Caution and close monitoring are advised. Ethionamide can also increase isoniazid levels through an unspecified interaction mechanism, requiring careful monitoring. Additionally, ethionamide may reduce the effectiveness of sodium picosulfate/magnesium oxide/anhydrous citric acid by altering metabolism, and co-administration with antibiotics may decrease the efficacy of these agents by disrupting colonic bacterial flora necessary for drug activation. Common side effects of ethionamide include gastrointestinal disturbances (e.g., nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, metallic taste, and increased salivation), postural hypotension, depression, dizziness, drowsiness, headache, peripheral neuropathy, psychosis, photosensitivity, rash, gynecomastia, hypoglycemia, impotence, anorexia, dyspepsia, and mouth sores. Severe adverse effects include elevated liver enzymes, hepatitis, optic neuritis, visual changes, thrombocytopenia, and rare but serious cutaneous reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), and acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP). If signs of severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARs) develop, the suspected drug(s) should be discontinued immediately, and appropriate treatment should be initiated. Ethionamide should not be used as monotherapy for tuberculosis, as this can lead to rapid development of resistance. It must be combined with one or more companion drugs based on susceptibility testing results. Therapy may begin before susceptibility results are available, as deemed appropriate by the physician. Ethionamide may potentiate the adverse effects of other antituberculosis drugs when used concomitantly. Ophthalmologic examinations, including fundoscopy, should be performed before and periodically during therapy. Excessive alcohol consumption should be avoided, as it may increase the risk of psychotic reactions and liver damage. Ethionamide is contraindicated in patients with hypersensitivity to the drug or severe hepatic dysfunction. Caution is advised in patients with diabetes mellitus, thyroid disease, hepatic impairment, or HIV, as malabsorption syndrome may occur. Pregnant women should avoid using ethionamide, as it may harm the fetus. The effects of ethionamide on labor and delivery are unknown, and it is unclear whether the drug passes into breast milk. Ethionamide is metabolized in the liver and excreted by the kidneys. It may exhibit bacteriostatic or bactericidal activity depending on the concentration. Patients should take ethionamide orally, with or without food, as directed by their physician. If gastrointestinal upset occurs, taking the medication with meals or dividing the daily dose into smaller doses may help. Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) may be prescribed to prevent nerve-related side effects. Patients should complete the full prescribed course of ethionamide and other tuberculosis medications, even if symptoms improve. Regular monitoring of blood glucose levels is essential, especially in diabetic patients, as ethionamide may lower blood sugar. Symptoms of hypoglycemia, such as sweating, shaking, rapid heartbeat, hunger, blurred vision, dizziness, or tingling in the hands or feet, should be reported to a doctor immediately. Drug interactions may alter the effectiveness of ethionamide or increase the risk of side effects. Patients should inform their healthcare provider of all medications and supplements they are taking. In case of overdose, emergency medical attention should be sought immediately. Routine laboratory tests, including sputum tests, liver and thyroid function tests, blood glucose levels, and complete blood counts, should be conducted during therapy. Missed doses should be taken as soon as remembered unless it is close to the time of the next dose, in which case the missed dose should be skipped. Ethionamide should be stored at room temperature, away from light and moisture, and not in the bathroom. Expired or unused medication should be discarded properly. This information is a summary and does not include all possible details about ethionamide. Patients should consult their healthcare provider for complete information tailored to their specific health needs.
